story: Son of Oeneus and Althaea, and brother of Deianira. He led the hunt for the Calydonian boar and killed it, and gave the hide to Atalanta, the huntress he loved. His uncles took it from her, and he killed them. His mother, to avenge her brothers, burned the log his life depended on.
versions: Homer: Phoenix tells his story to Achilles, as a man whose anger nearly cost his city; his mother’s curse brings his death. In the underworld he asked Heracles to marry his sister Deianira.

name: Atalanta
tagline: Drew the boar’s first blood, and lost a race to three apples.
story: A huntress, left on a mountain as a baby and suckled by a bear. She drew first blood from the Calydonian boar, and Meleager gave her the prize. She would marry only a man who could outrun her, and those who lost were killed; Melanion (Hippomenes in Ovid) won by dropping three golden apples from Aphrodite, which she stopped to pick up.
versions: Apollodorus: her son Parthenopaeus was by Melanion, or by Ares. Hyginus: by Meleager.

transformation.text: A lioness, with her husband, for lying together in a god’s sanctuary

name: Adrastus
tagline: Led seven against Thebes, and came home alone.
story: King of Argos. An oracle told him to yoke his daughters to a boar and a lion; when two exiles came to his door fighting at night, Polynices with a lion on his shield and Tydeus with a boar, he married them to his daughters, and promised to win back their kingdoms. He led seven champions against the seven gates of Thebes. All were killed but him; his horse Arion, a son of Poseidon, carried him away. Ten years later the sons of the Seven took Thebes, and his own son was the only one to die.

name: Amphiaraus
tagline: Knew he would die at Thebes, and went anyway.
story: A seer and a warrior of Argos, married to Eriphyle, Adrastus’ sister. He foresaw that every one of the Seven but Adrastus would die, and would not go; but he had sworn to let his wife decide any quarrel with Adrastus, and Polynices bribed her with the necklace of Harmonia. Before he left, he told his sons to kill their mother. Fleeing from the battle, he was about to be speared in the back when Zeus split the earth with a thunderbolt, and it swallowed him, chariot and all.

immortal.text: Made immortal by Zeus; he gave oracles from under the earth at Oropus

name: Eriphyle
tagline: Sold her husband for a necklace.
story: Sister of Adrastus, and wife of Amphiaraus. Polynices gave her the necklace of Harmonia, Cadmus’ wedding gift to his bride, to send her husband to war; ten years later Thersander gave her Harmonia’s robe, and she sent her sons too. Her son Alcmaeon killed her for it.
versions: Homer: ‘hateful Eriphyle, who took precious gold for the life of her husband’.

name: Tiresias
tagline: Lived as a woman for seven years, and saw too much.
story: The blind seer of Thebes, who lived for seven generations, from Cadmus to the fall of the city. Asked by Zeus and Hera who takes more pleasure in love, he answered: the woman, nine parts to one; Hera blinded him, and Zeus gave him prophecy. He told Oedipus who had killed Laius, and Creon that he must bury Polynices. In the underworld he alone kept his mind, and told Odysseus how to get home.
versions: Apollodorus and Ovid: Hera blinded him, and Zeus gave him prophecy and a long life. Apollodorus also tells that Athena blinded him, for seeing her bathe.

transformation.text: A woman for seven years, after he struck two snakes mating, and a man again after striking them once more

name: Haemon
tagline: Died with the girl his father condemned.
story: Son of Creon, betrothed to Antigone. When his father sentenced her to be walled up alive, he begged for her life, and was refused. He found her hanged in the tomb, lunged at his father with his sword, missed, and killed himself across her body.
versions: Apollodorus: the Sphinx killed him, years before. Hyginus: he hid Antigone and they had a son; when Creon found out, Haemon killed her and himself.

name: Tydeus
tagline: Small, fierce, and ate his enemy’s brains.
story: Son of Oeneus, and half-brother of Meleager and Deianira, exiled from Calydon for killing a kinsman. Adrastus married him to his daughter Deipyle. Small in body, he was one of the Seven, and at Thebes he was mortally wounded by Melanippus. Athena was bringing him a medicine from Zeus that would make him immortal; but Amphiaraus, who hated him, cut off Melanippus’ head and gave it to him, and Tydeus split it open and ate the brains. Athena turned away in disgust, and let him die.
versions: Homer: Athena loved him, and he was ‘small in stature, but a fighter’.

name: Deipyle
tagline: Married to a boar.
story: Daughter of Adrastus, married to Tydeus, and mother of Diomedes.

name: Argia
tagline: Married to a lion.
story: Daughter of Adrastus, married to Polynices, and mother of Thersander.

name: Capaneus
tagline: Swore not even Zeus could stop him.
story: One of the Seven, a giant of a man, who boasted that he would burn Thebes whether Zeus willed it or not. He climbed a ladder onto the wall, and Zeus struck him down with a thunderbolt.

name: Evadne
tagline: Leapt into her husband’s funeral fire.
story: Daughter of Iphis, and wife of Capaneus. When the Argive dead were recovered and burned, she threw herself onto her husband’s pyre, and burned with him.

name: Parthenopaeus
tagline: A boy with a girl’s face, and his mother’s bow.
story: Son of Atalanta, the youngest and most beautiful of the Seven, with a face like a girl’s, as his name says. He carried a shield showing the Sphinx, and was killed at the gate he attacked.
versions: Apollodorus: son of Melanion, or of Ares. Hyginus: son of Meleager.

name: Diomedes
tagline: Wounded two gods in one day.
story: Son of Tydeus and Deipyle. Ten years after his father died at Thebes, he was one of the Epigoni, the sons of the Seven, who took the city. At Troy, with Athena beside him, he wounded Aphrodite in the hand and Ares in the belly, and with Odysseus he stole the Palladium and killed Rhesus in the night. Coming home, he found his wife unfaithful, because Aphrodite had not forgotten.
versions: The Cypria: he helped Odysseus drown Palamedes. Pindar: Athena made him immortal.

name: Alcmaeon
tagline: Killed his mother as his father told him, and was hunted for it.
story: Son of Amphiaraus and Eriphyle. He led the Epigoni against Thebes, and won. Then, as his father had told him, he killed his mother. Her Erinyes drove him mad, and he wandered from land to land looking for one that had not seen the sun when he killed her. He found it in silt at the mouth of a river, and was killed there for the necklace of Harmonia, which he had given away twice.

name: Thersander
tagline: Took back his father’s city, and paid his grandmother’s price again.
story: Son of Polynices and Argia. To make Alcmaeon lead the Epigoni, he bribed Eriphyle with the robe of Harmonia, as his father had bribed her with the necklace. The Epigoni took Thebes, and he became king there. He sailed for Troy and was killed on the way, in Mysia, by Telephus.

name: Glaucus of Corinth
tagline: Son of Sisyphus, and father of a hero, or not.
story: Son of Sisyphus, and king of Corinth after him. His son Bellerophon was the greatest hero of the city, though many said the boy’s real father was Poseidon.

name: Iobates
tagline: Read a letter asking him to kill his guest, and tried.
story: King of Lycia. His son-in-law Proetus sent him a young man with a sealed letter that asked him to kill its bearer. Not wanting to kill a guest himself, he sent Bellerophon against the Chimera, then against the Solymi and the Amazons, and set an ambush for him. When Bellerophon survived it all, Iobates showed him the letter, gave him his daughter, and half his kingdom.
versions: Homer does not name him: ‘the king of wide Lycia’.

name: Proetus
tagline: Believed his wife, and sent his guest away to die.
story: King of Tiryns, who took in Bellerophon when he came as an exile. When his wife told him the young man had tried to seduce her, he would not kill a guest, and sent him to his father-in-law in Lycia with a letter asking for his death.
versions: Apollodorus: twin brother of Acrisius, Danaë’s father, with whom he fought even in the womb.

name: Stheneboea
tagline: Wanted her guest, and when he refused, accused him.
story: Daughter of the king of Lycia, and wife of Proetus. She fell in love with Bellerophon; when he refused her, she told her husband he had tried to seduce her.
versions: Homer calls her Anteia. Euripides: Bellerophon came back on Pegasus, offered to carry her away, and dropped her into the sea.

name: Philonoe
tagline: Her father tried to kill the man he married her to.
story: Daughter of Iobates. Her father gave her to Bellerophon when he could not kill him, and she bore him Isander, Hippolochus and Laodamia.
versions: Homer leaves her unnamed.

name: Bellerophon
tagline: Killed the Chimera from the sky, and fell from it.
story: Son of Glaucus, or of Poseidon. Exiled from Corinth for a killing, he came to Proetus in Tiryns, whose wife fell in love with him and, when he refused her, accused him. Proetus sent him to Lycia with a letter asking for his death. Athena gave him a golden bridle, and on the winged horse Pegasus he killed the Chimera, beat the Solymi and the Amazons, and won the king’s daughter. At the height of his fortune he tried to ride Pegasus up to Olympus, and fell; he wandered alone after that, hated by the gods.
versions: Homer: no Pegasus; the gods sent signs, and his fall is told only as grief, after Ares and Artemis killed two of his children.

name: Pegasus
tagline: Sprang from a severed neck, and carries Zeus’s thunder.
story: Son of Poseidon and Medusa, who sprang from her neck when Perseus cut off her head, with his brother Chrysaor. Bellerophon caught him drinking at the spring of Peirene in Corinth, with a golden bridle from Athena, and rode him against the Chimera.

immortal.text: Flew up to the gods, and lives in the house of Zeus, carrying his thunder and lightning

name: Chimera
tagline: A lion in front, a snake behind, a goat in the middle, breathing fire.
story: A fire-breathing monster, lion in front, serpent behind and goat in between, that ravaged Lycia. Bellerophon shot her down from the back of Pegasus.
versions: Hesiod: a daughter of Echidna, sister of Cerberus and the Hydra.

name: Hippolochus
tagline: Told his son always to be the best.
story: Son of Bellerophon and Philonoe, and father of Glaucus. He sent his son to Troy with one piece of advice: always to be the best, and not to shame his fathers.

name: Laodamia
tagline: Bore Zeus a son, and was killed by Artemis.
story: Daughter of Bellerophon. Zeus lay with her, and she bore him Sarpedon. Artemis, in anger, killed her.

name: Glaucus of Lycia
tagline: Traded gold armour for bronze, out of friendship.
story: Son of Hippolochus, and grandson of Bellerophon, a leader of the Lycians at Troy with his cousin Sarpedon. Meeting Diomedes in battle, he told him his family’s story; they found that their grandfathers had been guest-friends, refused to fight, and exchanged armour, Glaucus giving gold for bronze.

name: Sarpedon
tagline: A son of Zeus, whom Zeus let die.
story: Son of Zeus and Laodamia, king of the Lycians and the bravest of Troy’s allies. When Patroclus came out in Achilles’ armour, Sarpedon stood against him. Zeus wanted to save him, but Hera said the other gods would want the same for their sons; Zeus wept tears of blood, and let him die. Sleep and Death carried his body home to Lycia.
versions: Hesiod and Apollodorus: a son of Zeus and Europa, brother of Minos; in Apollodorus, Zeus let him live three generations.

name: Patroclus
tagline: Went to war in his friend’s armour, and died for it.
story: Son of Menoetius, raised with Achilles in the house of Peleus. When Achilles refused to fight, Patroclus begged to lead his men in his armour. He drove the Trojans back from the ships and killed Sarpedon, then chased them to the walls, where Apollo stunned him and Hector killed him. Achilles came back to the war to avenge him.

name: Asterion
tagline: Raised the three sons Zeus left with his wife.
story: King of Crete. He married Europa after Zeus had brought her to the island, and raised her three sons by Zeus, Minos, Rhadamanthys and Sarpedon, as his own. When he died childless, Minos took the throne.

name: Rhadamanthys
tagline: So just in life that he judges the dead.
story: Son of Zeus and Europa, and brother of Minos. He gave the Cretans their laws, and was so just that after death he became a judge in the underworld, or a king in the Elysian Fields, where the gods send their favourites. Driven from Crete, he settled in Boeotia and married Alcmene, the mother of Heracles, after Amphitryon’s death.
versions: Homer: he lives at the end of the world, in the Elysian plain, where life is easiest for men.

name: Catreus
tagline: Sent his children away to escape an oracle, and met his son anyway.
story: Son of Minos and Pasiphae. An oracle said one of his children would kill him. His son Althaemenes fled to Rhodes to avoid it; his daughters he gave to Nauplius to be sold abroad. In old age he sailed to Rhodes to give his kingdom to his son; the herdsmen took him for a pirate, and Althaemenes, not knowing him, killed him with a spear.
versions: Euripides: he caught Aerope with a slave, and gave her to Nauplius to be drowned; Nauplius spared her.

name: Deucalion
tagline: Son of Minos, father of a king at Troy.
story: Son of Minos and Pasiphae, and father of Idomeneus, who led the Cretans to Troy.
versions: Not Deucalion of the flood.

name: Daedalus
tagline: Built a cow, a labyrinth and wings, and lost his son to the sky.
story: The greatest craftsman of Athens, of the house of Erechtheus. Jealous of his nephew’s talent, he threw him off the Acropolis, and fled to Crete. There he built Pasiphae a hollow wooden cow, and the Labyrinth to hold the child she bore; he gave Ariadne the thread. Minos kept him prisoner, so he made wings of feathers and wax for himself and his son Icarus, and they flew away. Icarus fell; Daedalus reached Sicily, and Minos followed him there to his death.
versions: Apollodorus: son of Metion, a son of Erechtheus.

name: Icarus
tagline: Flew too close to the sun.
story: Son of Daedalus. His father made him wings of feathers set in wax, and told him to fly neither too low, where the sea would wet the feathers, nor too high, where the sun would melt the wax. He flew higher and higher, the wax melted, and he fell into the sea that bears his name.

name: Perdix
tagline: Invented the saw, and was thrown off the Acropolis for it.
story: Son of Daedalus’ sister, and his apprentice. At twelve he invented the saw, copying the spine of a fish, and the compass. Daedalus, jealous, threw him from the Acropolis.
versions: Apollodorus calls him Talos, and has no bird.

transformation.text: A partridge, which keeps low to the ground for fear of heights

name: Cocalus
tagline: Hid a fugitive, and boiled his pursuer.
story: King in Sicily, who took in Daedalus. Minos, searching for him, carried a spiral shell from city to city and offered a reward to anyone who could pass a thread through it; Cocalus gave it to Daedalus, who tied the thread to an ant. Minos knew then that Daedalus was there. Cocalus promised to hand him over, and while Minos was in his bath, his daughters poured boiling water over him.

name: Glaucus
tagline: Drowned in a jar of honey, and brought back.
story: Son of Minos and Pasiphae. As a child, chasing a mouse, he fell into a jar of honey and drowned. The seer Polyidus found him, and Minos shut the seer in the tomb with the body until he brought the boy back to life.
versions: Apollodorus also tells that Asclepius raised him.

name: Polyidus
tagline: Raised the dead with a snake’s herb.
story: A seer from Argos. He found Minos’ drowned son by watching an owl drive bees from a cellar. Shut in the tomb with the body, he killed a snake that crept towards it; a second snake came, and brought a herb that revived the first. Polyidus laid the herb on Glaucus, and he rose. Minos made him teach the boy prophecy; as he sailed away, he told Glaucus to spit in his mouth, and the boy forgot everything.

name: Clymene
tagline: Sold abroad by her father, and married to the man sent to sell her.
story: Daughter of Catreus. Her father gave her and her sister Aerope to Nauplius to sell in a foreign land; Nauplius married her himself, and she bore him Palamedes.

name: Nauplius
tagline: Lit false fires on the rocks, to avenge his son.
story: Son of Poseidon, a sailor and wrecker of Euboea. Catreus gave him his daughters to sell abroad, and he married one of them. When the Greeks at Troy stoned his son Palamedes, he went round Greece persuading their wives to take lovers, and when the fleet sailed home, he lit beacons on the rocks of Cape Caphareus, and the ships ran aground.

name: Althaemenes
tagline: Fled an oracle across the sea, and fulfilled it there.
story: Son of Catreus. Told by an oracle that he would kill his father, he fled to Rhodes. Years later he killed a stranger landing on the shore, and learned it was Catreus. He prayed that the earth would swallow him, and it did.

name: Idomeneus
tagline: Grandson of Minos, who led eighty ships to Troy.
story: Son of Deucalion, and grandson of Minos, king of Crete. He had been one of Helen’s suitors, and led the Cretans to Troy with eighty ships; older than most, he was among the bravest of the Greeks, and he came home safely.
versions: Homer: he brought all his men home. Later writers: he vowed to sacrifice the first thing he met if he came home safe, and it was his son.

name: Talos
tagline: A man of bronze, with one vein, stopped with a nail.
story: A giant of bronze who guarded Crete, running round the island three times a day and stoning any ship that came near. A single vein ran from his neck to his ankle, closed with a bronze nail. When the Argo came, Medea drugged him, or promised him immortality and pulled out the nail, and his ichor ran out.
versions: Apollodorus: he was the last of the bronze race of men, or a gift of Hephaestus to Minos; some said Poeas shot him in the ankle.

name: Inachus
tagline: The river who judged between Hera and Poseidon.
story: Son of Ocean and Tethys, the river of Argos and its first king. When Hera and Poseidon both claimed the land, he judged it with two other rivers, Cephisus and Asterion, and they gave it to Hera. Poseidon dried up their waters, so that they run only after rain.
versions: In the tragedians and Apollodorus, Inachus is Io’s father; Hesiod, as Apollodorus reports, makes her the daughter of Peiren.

name: Io
tagline: Loved by Zeus, turned into a cow, and driven across the world.
story: Daughter of Inachus and priestess of Hera. Zeus loved her, and when Hera found them he turned Io into a white cow and swore he had never touched her. Hera asked for the cow, and set hundred-eyed Argus to guard her. After Hermes killed Argus, Hera sent a gadfly, and Io ran maddened through Europe and Asia, across the strait that bears her name, the Bosporus, to Egypt. There she took back her form and bore Epaphus by the Nile.
versions: Apollodorus: Zeus turned her into a cow; others say Hera did. In Aeschylus she meets Prometheus chained on his rock, and he foretells her wandering and her descendants.

transformation.text: Turned into a white heifer, and back into a woman in Egypt.

immortal.text: Worshipped in Egypt as the goddess Isis.

name: Argus
tagline: Saw everything, and slept with only half his eyes.
story: A giant with eyes all over his body, set by Hera to watch Io. Hermes lulled him with his pipes and stories and killed him, at Zeus’ bidding. Hera set his eyes in the tail of her peacock.
versions: Apollodorus: Argus is earth-born, or a son of Arestor; Hermes killed him with a stone. Ovid: Hermes sent him to sleep, then cut off his head; Hera put his eyes in the peacock’s tail.

name: Epaphus
tagline: Born of a touch of Zeus’ hand, by the Nile.
story: Son of Zeus and Io, born in Egypt; his name means ‘touch’, for Zeus made Io whole again with a touch. Hera had the Curetes carry him off, and Io searched for him as far as Syria. He became king of Egypt and founded Memphis, named after his wife.

name: Libya
tagline: Gave her name to Africa.
story: Daughter of Epaphus and Memphis. Poseidon loved her, and she bore him twins, Agenor and Belus. The land of Libya, all of Africa west of Egypt, is named after her.

name: Belus
tagline: Father of the twins whose fifty children were made to marry.
story: Son of Poseidon and Libya, twin of Agenor. He stayed in Egypt and ruled there, married Anchinoe, a daughter of the Nile, and had the twins Aegyptus and Danaus.

name: Agenor
tagline: Sent his sons after Europa, and told them not to come back without her.
story: Son of Poseidon and Libya, twin of Belus. He went to Phoenicia and reigned there. When Zeus carried off his daughter Europa, he sent his sons to find her and forbade them to return until they did. None of them came back.
versions: Homer calls Europa a daughter of Phoenix, not Agenor.

name: Danaus
tagline: Gave his fifty daughters daggers for their wedding night.
story: Son of Belus, twin of Aegyptus, who ruled Libya. Fearing his brother’s fifty sons, he built the first ship, by Athena’s advice, and fled with his fifty daughters to Argos, where the king gave up the throne to him. The sons of Aegyptus followed and asked for the girls in marriage. Danaus agreed, and gave each daughter a dagger. The Greeks were called Danaans after him.
versions: Aeschylus’ Suppliants: the daughters flee the marriage, and Argos takes them in under King Pelasgus.

name: Aegyptus
tagline: Sent his fifty sons to marry their cousins.
story: Son of Belus, twin of Danaus. He conquered the land of the Melampodes and named it Egypt after himself. He had fifty sons, and wanted them to marry Danaus’ fifty daughters.

name: Danaids
tagline: Fifty brides, forty-nine murderers.
story: The fifty daughters of Danaus. Their cousins, the sons of Aegyptus, came to Argos to marry them, and their father gave each a dagger. On the wedding night they killed their husbands, all but Hypermnestra. They buried the heads at Lerna, and Athena and Hermes purified them at Zeus’ command. Danaus then gave them to the winners of a footrace.
versions: Later writers say that in Hades they carry water for ever in jars that leak.
members_note: Apollodorus names all fifty, each with the cousin she married; Hyginus gives another list.

name: Sons of Aegyptus
tagline: Fifty bridegrooms, killed on their wedding night.
story: The fifty sons of Aegyptus. They followed their cousins to Argos, made Danaus agree to the marriage, and drew their brides by lot. Each was killed by his bride on the wedding night, all but Lynceus.
members_note: Apollodorus names all fifty, each with his bride.

name: Hypermnestra
tagline: The one bride who spared her husband.
story: Eldest of the daughters of Danaus. On the wedding night she spared Lynceus, because he had respected her maidenhood. Her father put her in chains, but she was later given back to Lynceus, and their son Abas ruled Argos.

name: Lynceus
tagline: The only bridegroom to wake up.
story: Son of Aegyptus, the one of the fifty whose bride spared him. He reigned in Argos after Danaus, with Hypermnestra.

name: Amymone
tagline: Went to find water, and found Poseidon.
story: One of the daughters of Danaus. Poseidon had dried up the springs of Argos, and Danaus sent her to look for water. She threw a dart at a deer and hit a sleeping satyr, who tried to rape her. Poseidon appeared and the satyr fled. She lay with Poseidon, and he showed her the springs of Lerna.

name: Abas
tagline: Father of the twins who fought over Argos.
story: Son of Lynceus and Hypermnestra, king of Argos. He married Aglaia and had the twins Acrisius and Proetus.

name: Cepheus
tagline: Chained his daughter to a rock to save his kingdom.
story: King of the Ethiopians. When the sea god sent a monster to punish his wife’s boast, the oracle of Ammon said he could be rid of it only by giving his daughter Andromeda to it. His people forced him, and he chained her to a rock by the sea. Perseus killed the monster and married her.
versions: Apollodorus: Euripides makes Cepheus and Phineus sons of Belus.

name: Cassiopeia
tagline: Said she was lovelier than the Nereids.
story: Wife of Cepheus, mother of Andromeda. She boasted that she was more beautiful than the Nereids, and they took it to Poseidon, who flooded the land and sent a sea monster.

name: Phineus
tagline: Came to claim his bride, and was turned to stone.
story: Brother of Cepheus, betrothed to his niece Andromeda. He did nothing to save her from the monster, and when Perseus had freed her, he plotted against him. Perseus showed him the Gorgon’s head, and he and his men were turned to stone.
versions: Ovid sets the fight at the wedding feast, with Phineus and his men bursting in.

name: Tartarus
tagline: As far below the earth as the sky is above it.
story: One of the first beings, after Chaos and Gaia: the misty pit as far beneath the earth as the sky is above it, where a bronze anvil would fall nine days to reach the bottom. Zeus shut the Titans there, and Typhon after them. With Gaia he fathered Typhon.

name: Pontus
tagline: Born of Gaia without love.
story: The barren sea, which Gaia bore by herself, without love, before she lay with Uranus. With his mother he fathered the old gods of the sea: Nereus, Phorcys and Ceto.

name: Nereus
role: The Old Man of the Sea
tagline: Never lied, and changed shape to avoid saying anything.
story: Eldest son of Pontus and Gaia, the truthful and gentle Old Man of the Sea. He married Doris, a daughter of Ocean, and had fifty daughters, the Nereids. Heracles seized him as he slept and held on while he turned into every kind of shape, until he told him where to find the apples of the Hesperides.

name: Phorcys
tagline: Father of the Gorgons, the Graeae and a dragon.
story: Son of Pontus and Gaia. With his sister Ceto he fathered the strangest brood in Hesiod: the grey-haired Graeae, the Gorgons, and the serpent that guards the golden apples.

name: Ceto
tagline: Mother of monsters.
story: Daughter of Pontus and Gaia, with a name that means ‘sea monster’. With her brother Phorcys she bore the Graeae, the Gorgons and the serpent Ladon, and perhaps Echidna too.

name: Typhon
tagline: Had a hundred snakes’ heads, and nearly took the sky.
story: Last child of Gaia, by Tartarus, born to avenge the Titans. From his shoulders grew a hundred snakes’ heads, and he spoke in the voices of bulls, lions and dogs. He would have ruled gods and men, but Zeus struck him with thunderbolts, burned all his heads, and threw him down into Tartarus. The winds of storm come from him.
versions: In the Homeric Hymn to Apollo, Hera bore Typhon alone, in anger at Zeus for bearing Athena without her. In Apollodorus, Typhon cut out Zeus’ sinews and hid them in a cave, before Zeus buried him under Mount Etna.

name: Echidna
tagline: Half a lovely nymph, half a speckled snake.
story: Above, a nymph with bright eyes and fair cheeks; below, a huge speckled serpent, eating raw flesh in a cave under the earth, immortal and never ageing. She lay with Typhon and bore Orthus, Cerberus and the Hydra.
versions: In Hesiod her mother is probably Ceto, though the line may mean Callirhoe; in Apollodorus she is a daughter of Tartarus and Gaia. Argus is said to have killed her as she slept.

name: Graeae
tagline: Three sisters, one eye, one tooth.
story: Daughters of Phorcys and Ceto, grey-haired from birth. They shared one eye and one tooth between them, passing them hand to hand. Perseus stole the eye and would not give it back until they showed him the way to the nymphs who had the cap of darkness, winged sandals and wallet.
members_note: Hesiod names two; Apollodorus adds a third.

name: Gorgons
tagline: A face that turned men to stone.
story: Three sisters who lived beyond Ocean, near the Hesperides, with heads wreathed in snakes, tusks like boars’, hands of bronze and golden wings. Whoever looked at them was turned to stone. Two were immortal and never aged; only Medusa could die.
members_note: Hesiod and Apollodorus agree on the three names.

name: Nereids
tagline: Fifty sisters of the sea, quick to take offence.
story: The fifty daughters of Nereus and Doris, who live with their father in the depths of the sea. Thetis, the mother of Achilles, is one of them, and so is Amphitrite, Poseidon’s wife. When Cassiopeia boasted she was lovelier than all of them, they took it to Poseidon.
members_note: Hesiod names all fifty; Homer gives a list of his own in the Iliad.

name: Ladon
role: The serpent of the golden apples
tagline: Never slept, and spoke with a hundred voices.
story: The great serpent that coils around the tree of the golden apples, at the edge of the world, in the garden of the Hesperides. In Apollodorus he has a hundred heads and speaks with many different voices.
versions: Hesiod: a child of Phorcys and Ceto. Apollodorus and Hyginus: a child of Typhon and Echidna.

name: Chrysaor
tagline: Sprang from Medusa’s neck, holding a golden sword.
story: When Perseus cut off Medusa’s head, Chrysaor sprang from her neck together with the winged horse Pegasus, both sons of Poseidon. His name means ‘golden sword’. He married Callirhoe, a daughter of Ocean, and fathered three-bodied Geryon.

name: Orthus
tagline: The two-headed dog who guarded the red cattle.
story: Son of Typhon and Echidna, brother of Cerberus, a dog with two heads. He guarded the red cattle of Geryon on the island of Erytheia, far in the west, with the herdsman Eurytion. Heracles killed him with his club.
versions: Hesiod makes him the father of the Sphinx and the Nemean lion; the mother is unclear, the Chimera or Echidna.

name: Geryon
tagline: Three men from the waist up, and one below.
story: Son of Chrysaor and Callirhoe, with three bodies joined at the waist. He kept his red cattle on Erytheia, beyond the Ocean stream. Heracles came for them as his tenth labour, killed his dog Orthus and herdsman Eurytion, and shot Geryon with his arrows.
versions: Stesichorus told his death in a long poem, the Geryoneis, from Geryon’s side.

name: Nemean Lion
tagline: No weapon could pierce its hide.
story: A lion reared by Hera and set loose on the hills of Nemea, with a hide no weapon could pierce. Heracles’ arrows bounced off it, so he trapped it in its cave and choked it with his arms. He wore its skin ever after. This was his first labour.
versions: Hesiod: a child of Orthus, by the Chimera or by Echidna. Apollodorus: a child of Typhon.

name: Hydra
tagline: Grew two heads for every one cut off.
story: Daughter of Typhon and Echidna, reared by Hera in the swamp of Lerna to harm Heracles. She had nine heads, one of them immortal, and for every head Heracles struck off, two grew back. His nephew Iolaus burned the stumps with torches, and Heracles buried the immortal head under a rock. He dipped his arrows in her poison.
versions: Hesiod gives no number of heads; Apollodorus nine; others more. Apollodorus adds that Hera sent a crab to bite Heracles’ foot.

name: Cerberus
tagline: Fawns on those who come in, eats those who try to leave.
story: Son of Typhon and Echidna, the dog who guards the house of Hades. He wags his tail at the dead as they enter, and devours anyone who tries to leave. For his last labour Heracles went down, mastered him with his bare hands, showed him to Eurystheus and took him back.
versions: Hesiod gives him fifty heads; Apollodorus three heads of a dog, a dragon’s tail, and snakes along his back.

name: Sphinx
tagline: Killed everyone who could not answer her riddle.
story: A monster with a woman’s face, a lion’s body and a bird’s wings, sent to Thebes by Hera. She sat on a mountain above the city and asked a riddle: what has one voice, and goes on four feet, then two, then three? Whoever failed she devoured. Oedipus answered: man. She threw herself from the citadel, and Thebes made him king.
versions: Hesiod: a child of Orthus, by the Chimera or by Echidna. Apollodorus and Hyginus: a child of Typhon and Echidna.

name: Erebus
tagline: The darkness under the earth.
story: Born of Chaos with his sister Night, the darkness that lies under the earth, on the way to the house of Hades. He lay with Night, and she bore Aether, the bright upper air, and Day.

name: Hypnos
tagline: Gentle to men, and once put Zeus himself to sleep.
story: Son of Night, twin brother of Death. He goes quietly over land and sea and is kind to men. At Hera’s request he put Zeus to sleep, so that she could help the Greeks at Troy, and afterwards he and his brother carried the body of Sarpedon home to Lycia.

name: Thanatos
tagline: Has a heart of iron, and lets no one go.
story: Son of Night, twin brother of Sleep, hateful even to the gods: whoever he seizes he holds. He came for Alcestis, who had agreed to die in her husband’s place, but Heracles wrestled him at her tomb and brought her back.
versions: Euripides: Heracles wrestles Death at the tomb. Apollodorus: Persephone sent Alcestis back, or, as some say, Heracles fought Hades.

name: Tityos
tagline: Laid hands on Leto, and vultures eat his liver.
story: A giant son of Gaia. When Leto passed through Panopeus on her way to Delphi, he tried to rape her. Her children shot him dead, and in the underworld he lies stretched over nine acres while two vultures tear at his liver.
versions: Apollodorus: his mother was Elara, a daughter of Orchomenus, whom Zeus hid under the earth, so that Earth brought the child to birth.

name: Ixion
tagline: Tried to seduce Hera, and was bound to a wheel for ever.
story: King of the Lapiths in Thessaly, the first man to kill a kinsman. Zeus pitied him, purified him and took him up to Olympus, where Ixion fell in love with Hera. Zeus shaped a cloud like her, and Ixion lay with it, and from that union came the Centaurs. Then Zeus bound him to a winged, fiery wheel that turns through the air for ever.
versions: Homer makes Pirithous a son of Zeus by Ixion’s wife; Apollodorus and Hyginus make him Ixion’s son.

name: Oeagrus
tagline: Father of Orpheus, at least in name.
story: A king of Thrace, sometimes called a river god. With the Muse Calliope he had Orpheus, the singer.

name: Eurydice
tagline: Followed her husband out of Hades, until he looked back.
story: Wife of Orpheus. Soon after the wedding she was bitten by a snake and died. Orpheus went down to the underworld and sang until Hades and Persephone let her go, on one condition: that he not turn round until they reached the light. Near the top he looked back, and she slipped away a second time.

name: Maenads
tagline: Tore apart a king and a singer.
story: The women who followed Dionysus into the mountains, dressed in fawnskins, carrying the thyrsus, mad with the god. In Thebes, led by Agave, they tore Pentheus to pieces. In Thrace they tore Orpheus apart, and his head floated down the river, still singing.
versions: Ovid: the women of the Ciconians killed Orpheus because he had turned away from women after Eurydice. Apollodorus says only that the Maenads tore him to pieces.
members_note: In Euripides’ Bacchae the three daughters of Cadmus lead the women of Thebes; the Thracian women who killed Orpheus have no names.

name: Pheres
tagline: Refused to die for his son.
story: Son of Cretheus and Tyro, brother of Aeson, founder of Pherae in Thessaly. When his son Admetus was granted a substitute in death, Pheres, old as he was, refused.

name: Admetus
tagline: Let his wife die in his place.
story: Son of Pheres, king of Pherae, an Argonaut. Apollo served him a year as a herdsman, as a punishment from Zeus, and was so fond of him that he won from the Fates the right for Admetus to escape death, if someone would die instead. His parents refused; his wife Alcestis agreed.

name: Alcestis
tagline: Died in her husband’s place, and came back.
story: The loveliest of the daughters of Pelias. Admetus won her by yoking a lion and a boar to a chariot, with Apollo’s help. When death came for him, she died in his place, and Heracles, his guest, wrestled Death at the tomb and brought her back veiled.

name: Eris
tagline: Threw the apple that started the Trojan War.
story: Daughter of Night, sister of Ares in Homer, small at first, then towering to the sky. She was the one god not invited to the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, and she threw among the guests a golden apple marked ‘for the fairest’. Hera, Athena and Aphrodite each claimed it, and Zeus sent them to Paris to judge.
versions: The apple and its inscription are in Apollodorus and Hyginus; the Cypria, as summarised by Proclus, says only that Eris started a quarrel among the goddesses about their beauty.

name: Neleus
tagline: Lost eleven of his twelve sons to Heracles.
story: Son of Poseidon and Tyro, twin of Pelias. Exposed at birth, the twins were raised by a herdsman, and later quarrelled; Neleus went south and founded Pylos. When he refused to purify Heracles, Heracles sacked Pylos and killed him with all his sons but Nestor, who was away.

name: Nestor
tagline: Old, wise, and fond of telling how things were done in his day.
story: The only son of Neleus to survive Heracles. He ruled Pylos for three generations of men and sailed to Troy in old age, the Greeks’ wisest counsellor. He came home safely, and Telemachus found him there, still telling stories.

name: Antilochus
tagline: Died to save his father.
story: Son of Nestor, young and fast, the dearest of Achilles’ friends after Patroclus. When Memnon attacked his father, whose horse had been shot, Antilochus stood in the way and was killed. Achilles avenged him.
versions: Homer and Pindar make Memnon his killer; Hyginus names Hector.

name: Memnon
tagline: Son of the Dawn, killed by the son of the sea.
story: Son of Eos and Tithonus, king of the Ethiopians, who came to help his uncle Priam wearing armour made by Hephaestus. He killed Antilochus, and Achilles killed him. His mother took his body away, and her tears are the morning dew.
versions: In the Aethiopis he is made immortal; Ovid tells instead how birds rose from his pyre and fought over it every year.

immortal.text: Zeus gave him immortality at his mother’s plea.

name: Penthesilea
tagline: Came to fight for Troy, and Achilles loved her as she died.
story: Daughter of Ares, queen of the Amazons. After Hector’s death she came to Troy with her warriors, and did great things in battle, until Achilles killed her. As he stripped her armour he fell in love with her, and when Thersites mocked him for it, Achilles killed Thersites too.

name: Poeas
tagline: Lit the pyre no one else would light.
story: Father of Philoctetes, an Argonaut, who shot down the bronze giant Talos. When Heracles lay on his pyre on Mount Oeta and no one would set it alight, Poeas did, and Heracles gave him his bow.
versions: Some say it was Philoctetes himself who lit the pyre.

name: Philoctetes
role: Archer with the bow of Heracles
tagline: Left on an island for ten years, then needed to win the war.
story: Son of Poeas, heir to the bow of Heracles. On the way to Troy a snake bit him, and the wound stank so much, and he cried out so much, that the Greeks left him on Lemnos. Ten years later the seer Helenus said Troy could not fall without the bow, and Odysseus fetched him back. Healed, he shot Paris.

name: Oileus
tagline: An Argonaut, and father of the lesser Ajax.
story: King of the Locrians and an Argonaut, father of Ajax the Lesser.

name: Ajax the Lesser
tagline: Dragged Cassandra from Athena’s altar.
story: Son of Oileus, leader of the Locrians, small, quick, in a linen breastplate, the best spearman after Achilles. On the night Troy fell he dragged Cassandra away from the image of Athena, to which she clung, and the image turned its eyes away. On his way home Athena wrecked his ship. He reached a rock and boasted he had escaped the sea in spite of the gods, and Poseidon split the rock and drowned him.

name: Chryses
tagline: Prayed for a plague, and got one.
story: Priest of Apollo at Chryse. He came to the Greek camp with a great ransom for his daughter, and Agamemnon sent him away with threats. He prayed to Apollo, and for nine days the god’s arrows brought plague on the Greeks.

name: Chryseis
tagline: The prize that started the quarrel of the Iliad.
story: Daughter of Chryses, taken in a raid and given to Agamemnon as his prize. He said he preferred her to his own wife. When Apollo’s plague forced him to give her back, he took Achilles’ prize, Briseis, instead.

name: Briseis
tagline: Taken from Achilles, and the cause of his anger.
story: A woman of Lyrnessus whose husband and brothers Achilles killed. He took her as his prize and loved her. When Agamemnon took her from him, Achilles withdrew from the fighting, and the Greeks began to lose. She was given back after Patroclus died, and mourned him, who had been kind to her.

name: Eetion
tagline: Father of Andromache, killed by Achilles.
story: King of Cilician Thebe, father of Andromache. Achilles sacked his city, killed him and his seven sons, but did not strip his body: he burned him in his armour and raised a mound over him.

name: Helenus
tagline: Told the Greeks how to take his own city.
story: Son of Priam and Hecuba, a seer, Cassandra’s twin in some accounts. When Paris was dead and Helen given to Deiphobus instead of him, Helenus left Troy, and Odysseus captured him. He told the Greeks that Troy could not fall without the bow of Heracles, the bones of Pelops and Achilles’ son.

name: Laocoon
tagline: Warned the Trojans about the horse.
story: A Trojan priest who warned against taking the wooden horse into the city. Two serpents came over the sea and killed him and one of his sons, and the Trojans took it as a sign that he had been wrong.
versions: The Iliou Persis says the serpents killed Laocoon and one son; Apollodorus says both sons, and that Apollo sent them.

name: Polydectes
tagline: Asked for a horse and was given the Gorgon’s head.
story: King of the island of Seriphos, where the chest carrying Danaë and her baby washed ashore. He wanted Danaë, and her grown son stood in the way, so he sent Perseus to fetch the head of Medusa. Perseus came back, found his mother hiding at the altars, and turned the king and his guests to stone.
versions: Apollodorus: Polydectes pressed Danaë and she fled to the altars with Dictys. Pindar speaks of her slavery and a forced marriage. Hyginus: Polydectes married Danaë and raised Perseus in a temple of Athena.

name: The sea monster
tagline: Came for a princess and met Perseus.
story: A sea monster sent by Poseidon against the land of Cepheus, after Queen Cassiopeia had boasted she was more beautiful than the Nereids. An oracle of Ammon said only Andromeda could buy it off, so she was chained to a rock by the sea. Perseus, flying back with the Gorgon’s head, killed it and married her.
versions: Apollodorus: Poseidon sent a flood and the monster. Hyginus: Poseidon demanded that Andromeda be given to the monster.
